lesson.title: Trading Time for Frequency: Living Entirely in the Phasor Domain
lesson.summary: The phasor domain replaces time-varying sinusoids with fixed complex numbers, letting every rule from AC circuit analysis operate purely algebraically before a final step converts the answer back into an actual time-domain waveform.
lesson.body:
The phasor domain is the alternate mathematical space where a sinusoid v(t) = Vm cos(wt + theta) is represented instead by a fixed complex number, V = Vm at angle theta, with no time variable inside it at all. All the timing information has not disappeared, it has simply been separated out: the phasor keeps only the amplitude and phase, while the shared angular frequency w is treated as a single external parameter that applies to the whole circuit at once. This only works because every source in a linear AC circuit at steady state oscillates at the same frequency, so w never needs to travel along with each individual phasor.

Think of the phasor domain the way you might think of a foreign currency exchange: you convert your time-domain quantities into phasors, do all your work, addition for KVL and KCL, multiplication by jwL or 1/(jwC) for inductors and capacitors, division for Ohm's law, entirely inside that domain, and only convert back to time-domain waveforms at the very end, if you need them at all. The conversion back uses v(t) = Re{V e^(jwt)}: the phasor's magnitude becomes the waveform's amplitude, and its angle becomes the phase added to wt inside the cosine.

The derivative rule is where the phasor domain earns its keep. For an inductor, v_L(t) = L di/dt in the time domain becomes, in the phasor domain, V_L = jwL I, multiplication instead of differentiation. Suppose an inductor with L = 0.2 H carries current i(t) = 5 cos(1000t - 30 degrees) A, so its phasor is I = 5 at angle -30 degrees A. The impedance jwL = j(1000)(0.2) = j200 = 200 at angle 90 degrees ohms, so V_L = 200 at 90 degrees times 5 at -30 degrees = 1000 at angle 60 degrees V. Converting back to the time domain gives v_L(t) = 1000 cos(1000t + 60 degrees) V.

That answer is worth checking directly with calculus, as a confidence check on the whole method. Differentiating i(t) = 5cos(1000t - 30 degrees) gives di/dt = -5000 sin(1000t - 30 degrees), so v_L = L di/dt = 0.2 times (-5000 sin(1000t-30 degrees)) = -1000 sin(1000t-30 degrees). Using the identity -sin(phi) = cos(phi + 90 degrees), this becomes 1000 cos(1000t - 30 + 90 degrees) = 1000 cos(1000t + 60 degrees), the exact same result the phasor shortcut gave, without ever writing a derivative. That agreement is the whole point: once a circuit is fully translated into the phasor domain, complete with impedances standing in for every element, the algebra of AC circuit analysis you just learned produces correct time-domain answers automatically, and you only need to leave the phasor domain once, at the finish line.

Looking back, the entire method from the previous section, replace sources with phasors, replace elements with impedances, apply KVL and KCL, was really a description of working inside the phasor domain the whole time without naming it directly. Naming it now matters because larger circuits, several loops, several nodes, several reactive elements, can get solved entirely as one algebraic system in this domain, using the same linear equation techniques from DC analysis, before a single cosine wave is ever written down.
